extracted.intended_audience: patent owners, potential petitioners, and IP counsel (patent litigators and prosecutors)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and procedural guidance on filing and defending Inter Partes Review (IPR), Post-Grant Review (PGR), and transitional business-method post-grant review under the AIA, including petition contents, thresholds, estoppels, trial process, fees, and strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter Partes Review — Applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: On and after September 16, 2012, inter partes review will be available as to any still-enforceable issued patent, subject to the limitations discussed (e.g., one-year bar, prior civil actions, estoppel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPR replaces inter partes reexamination and is limited to challenges under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 and 103 based on patents and printed publications. A patent is enforceable up to six years after it expires. Consider applicability limitations when planning challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter Partes Review — Who Can File
rubrics_metrics.description: Any third party (anyone who is not the owner of the challenged patent) can file a Petition for inter partes review, as long as certain exceptions do not apply (e.g., petitioner has filed a civil action challenging the patent; complaint served >1 year before filing; petitioner/real party/privy estopped).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of the one-year-from-service bar and prior civil actions that can preclude filing. 'Third party' is broad but estoppel and prior litigation can block availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter Partes Review — Time for Filing
rubrics_metrics.description: A Petition for inter partes review must be filed on or after September 16, 2012, and can only be filed after the later of (1) nine months after the issue date of the patent; or (2) if a post-grant review has been instituted, the date of termination of the post-grant review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing interacts with post-grant review and reexamination options; plan filings relative to issue date and other proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter Partes Review — Basis of Petition
rubrics_metrics.description: A Petition can only challenge claims under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 or 103 based on patents or printed publications. For patents subject to the new §§ 102/103, the Petition can only rely on patents or printed publications as those sections allow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPR does not permit challenges under §§ 101, 112, or 251, or reliance on public knowledge/public use/sale evidence. Confirm which statutory regime the patent falls under when selecting grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter Partes Review — Contents of Petition
rubrics_metrics.description: Per 37 C.F.R. §42.104 the Petition must (a) establish petitioner standing, (b) identify relief requested, and (c) identify for each challenged claim: the challenged claim; statutory basis (102/103) and cited patents/printed publications; claim construction; why claim is unpatentable with element-by-element support; exhibit numbers and specific portions relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petition must also identify real party in interest, related matters, counsel, and service information; may include statement of material facts; attach exhibits and English translations with affidavits. Petition limited to 60 double-spaced 14-point font pages (IPR). Use claim charts (single-spaced) to be concise. For §112(f) limitations, identify corresponding specification structure/material/acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter Partes Review — Claim Construction Expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules appear to require construing full breadth of each claim term, but USPTO applies 'broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification', giving plain meaning unless inconsistent with the specification; detailed constructions only needed for terms with special meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative proposed constructions are permissible; for means/step-plus-function limitations, identify corresponding specification portions. Consider effect of proposed constructions on later litigation and estoppels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter Partes Review — Threshold Standard for Institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Board will institute IPR if the Petition, unrebutted, demonstrates that 'there is a reasonable likelihood that at least one of the claims challenged in the Petition is unpatentable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO describes this as a flexible standard easier to meet than the PGR 'more likely than not' standard. Applied claim-by-claim and ground-by-ground. Board will consider Patent Owner Preliminary Response when deciding institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter Partes Review — Fee
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO fee for filing an IPR petition depends on number of challenged claims: $27,200 for up to 20 claims; $600 additional per claim over 20. No small or micro entity discount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims can be counted as multiple claims for fee purposes if claims they depend from are not challenged; multiple dependent claims counted as a single claim under some interpretations. Fees substantially higher than prior reexamination; consider staged fee structure changes in future rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter Partes Review — Estoppels: Petitioner/Real Party/Privies (35 U.S.C. §315(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a final decision of the Board is issued in an IPR, the petitioner, real party in interest, or privy will be estopped from challenging in a USPTO proceeding, civil action, or ITC proceeding any claim included in the final written decision on any ground that was raised during the IPR or that reasonably could have been raised during the IPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estoppel applies claim-by-claim and takes effect once Board issues final decision (within ~12–18 months after institution). 'Reasonably could have been raised' is undefined; USPTO commentary suggests it covers prior art a diligent skilled searcher could reasonably have found. The Board may deny subsequent petitions with same or substantially same art/arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter Partes Review — Definition of Real Party in Interest and Privy
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice Guide discusses 'real party in interest' as the party that desires review, and 'privy' as a party whose relationship is sufficiently close to be bound by trial outcome and estoppels; mere association alone is insufficient to establish privity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of privity is fact-specific; parties should evaluate relationships and potential estoppel exposure when planning involvement or funding of petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter Partes Review — Patent Owner Estoppel/Limitations on Subsequent USPTO Actions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is canceled as part of the final judgment in an IPR, the patent owner will be precluded from taking action in the USPTO inconsistent with that judgment, including obtaining a claim not patentably distinct from a finally refused or canceled claim or obtaining an amendment that was denied during the trial proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents patent owner from getting a second bite at the apple for lost claims or denied amendments; patentably distinct claims can be pursued in continuing or reissue applications. Substantive amendments or new claims may give rise to intervening rights under 35 U.S.C. §318(c) and doctrine of equitable intervening rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Grant Review — Applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: As of September 16, 2012, PGR is available for any issued patent that either (1) includes claims subject to the new §§ 102 and 103 (generally patents with earliest effective filing date on/after March 16, 2013) or (2) is eligible for the transitional post-grant review for business method patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PGR broadens available bases for challenge but is limited to patents within the new statutory regime or transitional program; evaluate eligibility before choosing PGR vs IPR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Grant Review — Who Can File
rubrics_metrics.description: Any third party (not the patent owner) can file a Petition for PGR, subject to exceptions: petitioner or real party has filed a civil action challenging validity; petitioner/real party/privy is estopped from challenging the claims on the grounds identified in the petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same standing considerations as IPR; check for prior litigations or estoppels that may block filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Grant Review — Time for Filing
rubrics_metrics.description: A Petition for PGR must be filed on or after September 16, 2012, and only on or before the date that is nine months after the issue date of the patent (with special rules for reissue patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PGR is only available in the early post-issuance window; plan to file within nine months of issuance if PGR is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Grant Review — Basis of Petition
rubrics_metrics.description: A PGR petition can challenge claims on any basis available under 35 U.S.C. §§ 282(b)(2) or (3): §§ 101, 102, 103, 112 (except best mode), and/or 251. Inequitable conduct is not a basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PGR allows broader challenges than IPR; consider whether broader grounds justify PGR despite higher fees and earlier filing deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Grant Review — Contents of Petition
rubrics_metrics.description: Per 37 C.F.R. §42.204 the Petition must (a) establish standing, (b) identify relief requested, and (c) identify for each challenged claim: challenged claim; statutory basis (101/102/103/112/251) and cited patents/printed publications; claim construction; why claim is unpatentable with element-by-element support; exhibits and specific portions relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petition must identify real party in interest, related matters, counsel, and service info; attach exhibits and English translations with affidavits. Petition limited to 80 double-spaced 14-point font pages (PGR). Claim charts encouraged. For §112(f) limitations identify corresponding specification portions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Grant Review — Claim Construction Expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: As in IPR, rules appear to require construing full breadth of claim terms but USPTO will apply 'broadest reasonable construction in light of the specification' and give plain meaning unless inconsistent; detailed constructions only where terms have special meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative constructions permissible; consider claim construction impact on institution and later litigation. Patent owner statements from court or USPTO proceedings may be submitted but considered only after institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Grant Review — Threshold Standard for Institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Board will institute PGR if the Petition, unrebutted, demonstrates that it is 'more likely than not that at least one of the claims challenged in the Petition is unpatentable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a higher standard than IPR's 'reasonable likelihood'. Applied claim-by-claim and ground-by-ground. Board may rarely institute under alternative standard for novel/unsettled legal questions of broad importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Grant Review — Fee
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO fee for filing a PGR petition depends on number of challenged claims: $35,800 for up to 20 claims; $800 additional per claim over 20. No small or micro entity discount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fees exceed prior reexamination; dependent and multiple dependent claims counted similarly to IPR. Consider cost tradeoffs and staged fee rulemaking possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Grant Review — Estoppels (Petitioner/Real Party/Privies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estoppols apply on a claim-by-claim basis once final decision of the Board is issued; because PGR covers broader grounds, the resulting estoppols are broader (apply to any arguments that were raised or reasonably could have been raised under §§ 101, 102, 103, 112 (except best mode), and/or 251).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broader estoppels counsel caution when choosing PGR: a PGR that addresses only 102/103 may still preclude later arguments under other statutes that reasonably could have been raised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional Post-Grant Review for Business Method Patents — Applicability/Who Can File/Qualifying Patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitional PGR permits petitioners to request PGR of certain patents directed to business methods that are otherwise ineligible for PGR; specifics include eligibility criteria for 'business method' patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a single claim meets the transitional standard, the entire patent can be subject to PGR; during prosecution consider separating business-method-like claims into separate continuations to limit exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional Post-Grant Review — Grounds for Challenging Patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitional PGR permits challenges under the applicable statutory grounds (consistent with PGR), subject to the AIA's special provisions for business-method patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check AIA-defined standards and statutory text for business-method scope and any special stay rules applicable to civil actions under the AIA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional Post-Grant Review — Estoppels and Stay of Infringement Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitional PGR imposes estoppels similar to PGR/IPR and establishes AIA standards courts use to determine stays of infringement actions when transitional PGR is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing or pendency of a transitional PGR can affect litigation strategy via stays; one-year from service bar and other timing rules remain relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial Process — Settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: An IPR or PGR can be terminated based upon a settlement agreement of the parties; if trial is terminated based on settlement, estoppols will not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing (or threatening to file) an IPR/PGR can be an effective negotiation tool because settlement can avoid estoppols; assess settlement as a strategy for both petitioners and patent owners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial Process — Petition (procedural role during trial)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Petition is the primary document presenting petitioner's arguments and evidence; the rest of the trial may focus on patent owner counter-arguments and petitioner's rebuttals rather than re-establishing the petition basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft a thorough, concise Petition with claim charts and supporting evidence; consider withholding limited information only with awareness of risks (e.g., claims not included in trial, deadline effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial Process — Optional Preliminary Patent Owner Response
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owner may file a Preliminary Patent Owner Response; the Board will take such response into account when deciding whether to institute trial. Patent owners must decide strategically whether and what substantive issues to include.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent owners may withhold substantive patentability arguments until after institution to avoid providing information that could be used as supplemental information for petitioners; weigh estoppel and tactical tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial Process — Institution of Trial; Scope of Institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Board may institute trial for all or some claims and on all or some grounds; institution is claim-by-claim, ground-by-ground, and the proceeding is generally limited to instituted claims/issues unless new issues are raised by supplemental information or claim amendments are filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners should consider which claims/grounds they want included because estoppols and scope are tied to instituted items; claim selection affects strategy and cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial Process — Scheduling Order, Preliminary Conference, and Supplemental Information
rubrics_metrics.description: After institution the Board issues a scheduling order and may hold a preliminary conference call; petitioners may file supplemental information post-institution under tight deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners can supplement information within short windows; patent owners should anticipate rapid proceedings and prepare for potential supplemental submissions and adjusted deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial Process — Patent Owner Response; Petitioner's Reply; Evidence and Motion Practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owner files a full response after institution; petitioner may reply. The proceeding includes evidence submission rules and motion practice governed by Board rules (motions to exclude, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect intensive motion practice and evidence disputes; prepare declarations, identify exhibits and likely witnesses early, and plan for timely exchange and admissibility challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial Process — Motion to Amend (patent owner)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owners can file motions to amend claims, but USPTO plans to limit number of claims that can be proposed; motions to amend are scrutinized and denials can create patent owner estoppels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent owners must carefully consider amendments in view of intervening rights, estoppel, claim differentiation effects, and third-party products/plans. Prepare proposed amendments early (outline by initial conference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial Process — Discovery (Mandatory Initial Disclosures, Routine Discovery, Additional Discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board provides for mandatory initial disclosures, routine discovery, and limited additional discovery governed by rules; discovery obligations and windows are short relative to district court litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should plan e-discovery, identify custodians/search terms, prepare for depositions and expert testimony within compressed schedules. Petitioners have advantage of pre-filing preparation; patent owners must mobilize quickly once aware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial Process — Protective Orders, Oral Hearing, Final Decision, Timing, Rehearing, Judicial Review, Sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings include mechanics for protective orders, an oral hearing opportunity, issuance of a final written decision by the Board (timelines ~12–18 months), requests for rehearing, appeal/judicial review paths, and potential sanctions for misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand timeline expectations, appellate standard differences with courts, and potential sanctions; plan communications, confidentiality, and preservation accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations — Availability and Reexamination as Alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-Grant Review will not be immediately available for many patents (those not subject to new §§ 102/103), and reexamination (ex parte or inter partes reexam until Sept 15, 2012) remains available and is less expensive but procedurally different (favours patent owner, no discovery, slower).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider reexamination for cost or timing reasons, especially if many claims are to be challenged or page limits would be exceeded; weigh procedural differences (no discovery) against objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations — One-Year From Service Bar
rubrics_metrics.description: IPR is not available to parties who were served a complaint alleging infringement more than one year before filing the Petition; the first complaint starts the one-year clock even if dismissed later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alleged infringers sued previously must evaluate options and may be limited to reexamination or other remedies; consider implications of serial suits and early strategic timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations — Claim Selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of which claims to challenge is strategically important and affects cost and estoppel; estoppols attach only to claims included in the final written decision, so selective challenge can preserve other claims for later challenge but may be risky.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selective challenges may be seen as attempts to reassert arguments later; USPTO and courts may deny or limit subsequent petitions or refuse equitable relief. Consider fees, dependent-claim counting for fees, and potential court views when selecting claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations — Grounds of Challenge (IPR vs PGR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in available grounds between IPR (only §§ 102/103 based on patents/printed publications) and PGR (§§ 101, 102, 103, 112 (except best mode), 251) affect both challenge opportunities and scope of estoppols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only 102/103 challenges are intended, often better to wait and file IPR nine months after issuance to avoid broader PGR estoppols; choose forum (USPTO vs court) and proceeding according to desired grounds and estoppel risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations — Thoroughness of Petition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Petition may be the primary presentation of petitioner's position; it should be thorough, concise, and include claim charts. The purpose is not merely to meet institution threshold but to present arguments and evidence that will carry through trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance thoroughness with page limits; withholding information is possible but risky (may cause claims not to be instituted or extend deadlines). Prepare as if Petition will be the core case record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations — Forum Selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Because standards of review, claim construction, and presumption of patentability differ between Board trials and federal court, petitioners should evaluate which forum best suits their arguments (e.g., broader constructions and lower burdens may favor Board).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider substantive and tactical advantages of IPR/PGR vs district court (burden of proof, claim construction standards, speed, discovery differences) when deciding where to challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations — Stay of Civil Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing an IPR or PGR before or soon after filing of an infringement action will likely result in a stay of the infringement action, though stays are within the court's discretion and vary by venue and timing; suits filed by petitioner prior to petition may bar IPR/PGR; suits filed after petition are subject to automatic stays under 35 U.S.C. §§ 315(a)(2) and 325(a)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use petitions tactically to obtain a stay or to shape litigation timetable, but be aware of one-year bar and prior suits that can preclude relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations — Early Planning and Preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Trials move quickly with discovery, testimony, and depositions within short windows; petitioners should prepare discovery, witnesses, e-discovery plans, mandatory disclosures, and other trial materials before filing; patent owners must mobilize promptly at first sign of petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners have a preparation advantage; litigants should identify experts, custodians, search terms, and draft potential claim amendments or replacement claims early (outline by initial conference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations — Settlement as Tactical Tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Because IPR/PGR can be terminated by settlement and estoppols do not apply if the trial is terminated by settlement, settlement can be an effective tool to avoid estoppols and to negotiate favorable outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider early settlement to avoid estoppols; use the threat of petition filing as negotiation leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations — Claim Construction Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner must construe challenged claims in the Petition; proposed constructions can affect subsequent litigation, licensing, and estoppel exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully consider proposed claim constructions and how they will influence later disputes and negotiations; avoid constructions that inadvertently harm broader strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations for Patent Owners — Early Planning and Preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owners will often not control whether they are drawn into an IPR/PGR and must move quickly to prepare for discovery, testimony, deposition, and potential amendments once a Petition is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin organizing evidence, identifying experts, preserving materials, and preparing possible claim amendments immediately when disputes arise or negotiations occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations for Patent Owners — Preliminary Patent Owner Response Strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owners must decide whether to file or what to include in a Preliminary Patent Owner Response; they may avoid substantive patentability content to prevent enabling petitioner's supplemental submissions and to preserve arguments for the full Patent Owner Response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider withholding substantive arguments in the Preliminary Response and reserve them for the Patent Owner Response after institution to reduce the risk of triggering supplemental filings or estoppel-related consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations for Patent Owners — Claim Amendment Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO plans to limit the number of claims a patent owner can present in a motion to amend. Patent owners must consider intervening rights, effect on remaining claims, patent owner estoppols, and competitors' products when proposing amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare proposed amendments early, balance protection vs intervening rights, and think about how added claims affect claim construction and differentiation.
